title: The Kotzker and emet
hookLine: the Kotzker rebbe demanded truth without comfort
carry: emet can't be imitated, only lived
last: TESHUVAH: IF YOU CAN DAMAGE, YOU CAN REPAIR.

cards: These last days have been warm ones. Joy that opens. A rebbe at the head of the table.
Pulling sadness into the dance. Today the temperature drops. In the small Polish town of Kotzk lived a Hasidic rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel, who had little patience for warmth that wasn't real.
Stories about him are sharp, short, and a little frightening. Tradition says he would rather have a handful of followers who were honest than crowds who were comfortable.
His whole life circled one word, and he wanted it without any padding.

teach.b: Truth. In Hebrew, emet. First, the Bible's standard.
The psalm asks who may dwell on God's holy mountain, and part of its answer is the one who "speaketh truth in his heart." Not only with the mouth. In the heart, where nobody checks.
Second, the sages. The Talmud teaches that God's seal is truth.

And it notices something about the word itself: emet is spelled with the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a letter from the middle, and the last. Truth, the sages suggest, runs the whole length, beginning to end.
Sayings attributed to him are passed on by his followers, and one of them goes like this: everything in the world can be imitated except truth, because truth that's imitated isn't truth anymore.
He aimed it first at religious life. Prayer done for show, piety performed for the neighbors, a warm feeling worn like a coat.
To him, those were imitations, and he'd take an honest struggle over a comfortable fake. Fourth, the cost, said fairly.

The Kotzker's way is hard, and Hasidic tradition itself remembers him as a fierce and solitary figure. Not every teacher walked his road, and the other Hasidic teachers in these lessons lean toward warmth and joy.
His question can sit underneath the warm paths too. Is this real?
Am I telling the truth in my heart, where nobody checks? That's what fiercely means here. Not cruelty to others.

how: Jewish teaching counts honesty, in speech and in the heart, among the basic demands of the Torah; the sayings of the Kotzker rebbe are retold in Hasidic and wider Jewish circles as a challenge to empty piety.

o: emet: what's real, with no padding or pretending
a promise that is sealed with a vow before God

s: the Kotzker's fierceness meant being harsh with other people
his demand was honesty with yourself, without padding, aimed first at his own world's piety.
emet is spelled with the first, a middle and the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet
the sages read it as truth running the whole length, beginning to end.
every Hasidic teacher walked the Kotzker's road
the other Hasidic teachers we've met lean toward warmth and joy. the Kotzker's road was fierce and solitary.

games.q: you're a follower in Kotzk. your prayer felt warm today, but you know part of it was for show. what would the Kotzker want?
o: keep the warm feeling and don't look too closely.
admit the part that was for show, and take the honest struggle.
games.why: tradition remembers him preferring an honest struggle over a comfortable imitation. truth that's imitated isn't truth.

practice: Ask yourself one plain question, and let the answer come without dressing it up: what am I pretending about?
Maybe a feeling you claim not to have, a habit you call fine, a reason that isn't the real one; when it comes, don't argue with it or punish yourself, just let it be true for a minute.
If you pray, you can stand before God with exactly that, and nothing extra.

wordCard.voice: Truth. Emet in Hebrew, God's seal for the sages, and for the Kotzker rebbe the one thing that can't be imitated. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: truth. Alef, mem, tav: the first letter, a middle one, and the last.

carryVoice: Your line: emet can't be imitated, only lived. Not cruelty to others: honesty with yourself. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Sayings of Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Kotzk (oral tradition)
